planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained, stony soil in full sun; Areni Noir is traditionally grown at high elevation in Armenia's Vayots Dzor province, so it tolerates cool nights well but still needs a long, dry, sun-soaked season to fully ripen its thin-skinned clusters.

directions: Train vines onto a permanent trellis or head-trained vineyard system and prune to open the canopy, since Areni Noir's thin skin is prone to rot if clusters stay damp or shaded. Named for the village of Areni near the Areni-1 cave in Vayots Dzor, where archaeologists uncovered what is considered the world's oldest known winemaking facility alongside ancient grape seeds and a wine press, this indigenous red variety produces light-to-medium-bodied, high-acid wines often compared to Pinot Noir or Nebbiolo for their perfume and structure. Harvest in mid-autumn once sugars and acidity balance, and expect a long ripening window given the variety's high-elevation origin around 3,000 to 5,000 feet. Modern Armenian producers have revived Areni Noir as the country's flagship export wine grape after centuries of mostly local, small-scale cultivation.
sources: Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and Jose Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes: A Complete Guide to 1,368 Vine Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Voskehat is grown mainly in Armenia's warmer, lower-elevation Ararat Valley, so it needs a longer, hotter season than high-elevation Armenian reds to fully ripen.

directions: Train onto a trellis or traditional head-trained vineyard system and thin crowded shoots to keep clusters well exposed to sun, since Voskehat sets heavy crops that can dilute flavor if left unmanaged. Its name translates roughly to 'golden grain,' describing the deep golden color its berries take on at full ripeness, and it is considered Armenia's most widely planted native white grape, long grown in the Ararat Valley for both dry, floral, stone-fruit-driven table wine and for distillation into Armenian brandy. Harvest in early-to-mid autumn once must weight and acidity are balanced for the intended style, picking slightly earlier for brandy base wine than for still wine. Voskehat has become a central variety in Armenia's modern wine revival, often bottled as a single-varietal white.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Kangun is a vigorous, heavy-cropping Ararat Valley variety that tolerates Armenia's hot, dry continental summers once established.

directions: Train onto a trellis and prune for an open canopy to manage Kangun's vigorous growth and heavy, reliable yields. Grown chiefly in Armenia's Ararat Valley, this white variety has historically been one of the principal grapes used as base wine for Armenian brandy production because of its favorable sugar-to-acid balance and productivity, though it is also vinified as a straightforward dry white. Harvest timing depends on end use: pick earlier, at higher acidity, for brandy distillation, and allow slightly longer hang time for table wine. Kangun remains a workhorse variety in Armenian viticulture, planted alongside Voskehat as one of the valley's traditional brandy grapes.
sources: Vitis International Variety Catalogue (VIVC), Julius Kuhn-Institut

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Nerkarat is grown in Armenia's Armavir and Ararat Valley lowlands and needs a full warm season to develop its deep color and ripeness.

directions: Train onto a trellis and keep fruiting zones open to sun and airflow to help the thin-skinned clusters ripen evenly. Nerkarat is a red Armenian grape prized for its unusually deeply colored skin and juice, which has made it valuable both as a standalone red wine grape and as a blending component used to deepen the color of lighter reds. Harvest in mid-to-late autumn once the berries reach full dark color and sugars peak, since underripe fruit yields thinner color and harsher tannin. Nerkarat is grown mainly in the Armavir and Ararat Valley lowlands alongside Armenia's white brandy grapes, forming part of the country's traditional red wine production.
sources: Vitis International Variety Catalogue (VIVC), Julius Kuhn-Institut
Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and Jose Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes: A Complete Guide to 1,368 Vine Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Mskhali is grown in Armenia's Armavir region and prefers the same long, hot, dry growing season as the valley's other traditional white varieties.

directions: Train onto a trellis and thin congested shoots so clusters ripen evenly in full sun. Mskhali takes its name from the Armenian word for 'pear,' a reference to the elongated, pear-like shape of its berries, and it is grown as a minor traditional white variety in Armenia's Armavir region, used both for local table wine and blended into brandy base wine alongside better-known varieties like Voskehat and Kangun. Harvest in early-to-mid autumn once sugars and acid reach the balance appropriate for the intended wine style. Because plantings are limited compared to Armenia's leading white grapes, Mskhali is mostly found in small vineyard blocks rather than large-scale commercial production.
sources: Vitis International Variety Catalogue (VIVC), Julius Kuhn-Institut

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Bayanshira is a long-cultivated Azerbaijani variety adapted to the hot, dry summers of the Caspian basin's wine regions.

directions: Train onto a trellis or head-trained system and prune to control vigor, since Bayanshira is a productive variety that can overcrop without management. One of Azerbaijan's most significant native white grapes, it is grown across the country's traditional wine districts such as Ganja-Gazakh and Shamakhi, where it is vinified into both dry table wine and sweeter, fuller-bodied dessert styles depending on harvest timing and sugar accumulation. Pick earlier for crisp dry wine and allow extended hang time on the vine for richer, higher-sugar styles. Bayanshira has long served as a workhorse variety in Azerbaijani viticulture, valued for reliable yields and adaptability across the region's varied vineyard sites.
sources: Vitis International Variety Catalogue (VIVC), Julius Kuhn-Institut

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Madrasa is grown across Azerbaijan's traditional red wine districts and, just across the border, in parts of southern Dagestan, tolerating hot, dry continental summers once established.

directions: Train onto a trellis and keep the fruiting zone open to sun and airflow to support even ripening of this thick-skinned red variety. Madrasa, also transliterated as Matrasa, is one of Azerbaijan's principal native red grapes, producing deeply colored, full-bodied, tannic red wines traditionally used both as a standalone varietal and as a blending grape for structure and color. Harvest in mid-to-late autumn once tannins soften and color development peaks, since picking too early can leave the wine overly astringent. Beyond Azerbaijan, small plantings persist across the border in Dagestan, reflecting the shared viticultural history of the eastern Caucasus and Caspian basin.
sources: Vitis International Variety Catalogue (VIVC), Julius Kuhn-Institut
Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and Jose Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes: A Complete Guide to 1,368 Vine Varieties
